title: Your Own Game
tagline: Pick an idea, build it start to finish, and share it with a friend.
successMessage: You picked the idea, you picked what stayed and what got thrown out, and you shipped it. Every single tool you used to build it — gravity, lists, collisions, a score, a menu, juice — you taught yourself, one small game at a time. That's the whole course. 🏆

steps.title: Build your own game, start to finish
steps.brief: This one's yours. No fixed steps, no reference solution, no auto-grader watching your sprites — just a blank stage and everything you've built with over the last seven modules. Pick an idea, however small, and ship it.
todo: Pick a genre — dodge things, catch things, jump and land, escape a maze, or something nobody's built yet.
Grab a launchpad below if you want one, or start from the blank canvas already in your editor.
Build until every box in the checklist is honestly true, then tick it off.
steps.starterCode:
from stage import Game, Sprite, Box, Ball, Text, random_number

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Your toolbox, all in one place. Delete this comment block once you don't
# need it any more.
#
#   Game(width, height, background)   the stage itself, make this first
#   Sprite(look, x, y, size, name)    an emoji character — "star", "robot", ...
#   Box(x, y, width, height, color)   a rectangle — floors, walls, platforms
#   Ball(x, y, radius, color)         a circle
#   Text(words, x, y, size, color)    words on the stage — scores, messages
#   random_number(low, high)          a random whole number, low to high
#
#   thing.touching(other)             True when two things overlap
#   thing.move(dx, dy)                shift by dx across, dy down
#   thing.hide() / thing.show()       for menus and start screens
#   thing.remove()                    take it off the stage for good
#
#   game.key_down("left"/"right"/"up"/"down"/"space")   is a key held right now
#   game.clamp_inside(thing)          keep something from leaving the stage
#   game.shake(frames, power)         rattle the whole screen for a moment
#   game.score / game.state / ...     stick ANY name you like straight onto game
#   game.stop()                       end the game — update() stops running
#
#   sprite.scale_x / scale_y          stretch or squash a sprite (1.0 = normal)
#   a list + a for loop               any number of enemies, stars, particles...
#   @game.every_frame                 marks the function that runs ~60x/second
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

player = Sprite("robot", x=240, y=180, size=40, name="player")


@game.every_frame
def update():
    if game.key_down("left"):
        player.x = player.x - 4
    if game.key_down("right"):
        player.x = player.x + 4
    if game.key_down("up"):
        player.y = player.y - 4
    if game.key_down("down"):
        player.y = player.y + 4
    game.clamp_inside(player)


game.start()
hints: Stuck on an idea? Sketch it on paper first: what does the player control? What do they avoid or collect? How do they win, and how do they lose?
The fastest game to finish is usually a remix, not an original: take Space Dodger and swap rocks for something else, or take Jump Quest and change what the platforms mean.

Every game in this course is built from the same handful of moves: a stored speed (dx/dy/vy), a list you loop over, a touching() check that reacts, and a score or state variable stuck onto game. Mix and match them.
If it's not fun yet, it's almost always the numbers, not the idea — speed, gravity, how many enemies, how big the hitboxes are. Change one number at a time and replay it.
Small and finished beats big and half-built. A tiny game with a start screen, an ending, and one good idea is a real game. An ambitious one with no ending isn't, yet.

templates.code:
from stage import Game, Sprite, Text, random_number

game = Game(width=480, height=360, background="#0B1020")

player = Sprite("robot", x=240, y=320, size=40, name="player")

falling = []
for i in range(6):
    thing = Sprite("rock", x=random_number(20, 460), y=random_number(-200, 0),
                    size=30, name="thing" + str(i))
    falling.append(thing)

game.score = 0
label = Text("Score: 0", x=16, y=16, size=20, color="#FFC93C")


@game.every_frame
def update():
    if game.key_down("left"):
        player.x = player.x - 5
    if game.key_down("right"):
        player.x = player.x + 5
    game.clamp_inside(player)

    for thing in falling:
        thing.y = thing.y + 4
        if thing.y > 380:
            thing.y = random_number(-200, 0)
            thing.x = random_number(20, 460)
            game.score = game.score + 1
            label.words = "Score: " + str(game.score)

        if player.touching(thing):
            label.words = "Game over! Score: " + str(game.score)
            game.stop()


game.start()

milestones: There's something the player directly controls with the keyboard.
There's a real way to lose — not just an endless sandbox with nothing at stake.
There's a score, timer, or counter, visible on screen, that actually changes.
It has at least one piece of juice — a squash/stretch, a particle burst, or a screen shake.
It has a start screen or a game-over screen (or both) using game.state.
You've played it start to finish at least once, on purpose, without editing the code mid-run.
You've shown it to someone else and watched them play it.
